description_full: Shutterstock, Inc. provides platform to connect brands and businesses to high quality content in North America, Europe, and internationally. The company offers image services consisting of photographs, vectors, and illustrations, which is used in visual communications, such as websites, digital and print marketing materials, corporate communications, books, publications, and others; footage services, including video clips, filmed by industry experts and cinema grade video effects in HD and 4K formats that are integrated into websites, social media, marketing campaigns, and cinematic productions; and music services comprising music tracks and sound effects, which are used to complement images and footage. It also provides 3 dimensional models consisting of 3D models used in various industries, such as advertising, media and video production, gaming, retail, education, design, and architecture; and generative AI content comprising images generated from algorithms trained with ethically sourced content. In addition, the company operates a collection of graphics interchange format visuals and stickers that supplies casual conversational content. It offers its services under the Shutterstock, Envato, Pond5, TurboSquid, PicMonkey, PremiumBeat, Splash News, and Bigstock brand names. The company serves corporate professionals and organizations, media and broadcast companies, and small and medium-sized businesses, and individual creators through digital, live sales, services, and client management channels. Shutterstock, Inc. was founded in 2003 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

Revenue per employee of $633K ranks in the above the sector median among Communication Services peers, improving at 15%/yr — growing workforce leverage. financial_summary: Shutterstock, Inc. is a micro-cap communication services business with a $110M market cap on $990M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 7% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $124M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.66× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.9% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 4.5×.

Management returns a meaningful 42.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 31% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Trading at a 89% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Trading near the bottom of its 52-week range — the market is offering a discount

Financial quality scores above most Communication Services peers

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Communication Services median (9%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.37x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-15.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 80% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 87% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 75% and a beta of 1.22, it amplifies market moves.
About $3.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash and 57% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 89% below its DCF fair value of $26.90, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.56 to $37.19 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Communication Services peers: P/E 3.3 vs 14.9, EV/EBITDA 2.7 vs 9.4 and P/FCF 0.9 vs 11.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 95% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an EBIT/EV of 29.2% (vs the 8% bar).
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.88).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow, or 6% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 3.66x, but high accruals (-8.9% of assets).
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 9.0% of revenue on R&D and 6.2% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.6x net debt to EBITDA ($178.2M of cash against $274.7M of debt), with interest covered 4.5x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.09 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.54 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 42% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.1% over 3 years, 8.2% over 5 years and 8.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 12%).
At current returns, reinvesting 70% of profits supports about 11.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -2.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 4% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 6%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (4.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 31.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 53%.
It returns 42.4% a year to shareholders.
It pays out 106% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 1,565 employees, each generates about $633K of revenue, in line with the Communication Services median, and productivity has risen 14.5% a year.
That works out to $79K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
Compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
